paper.title: Tax bunching, income shifting and self-employment
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement. The acknowledgments state: …

registers.role: treatment (marginal tax rates and bracket cutoffs, via the authors' tax simulator), outcomes (personal/taxable income, earned income, retained and withdrawn earnings, transfers to assisting spouses, pension contributions) and sample frame
variables_mentioned: net profits under the firm tax scheme

registers.name_in_paper: the IDA database (Integrated Database for Labor Market Research)
the Tax Ministry's figures based on their 3.3 percentage representative sample
registers.role: aggregate retained and withdrawn earnings for the pre-1994 part of Fig. 3

linkages: Spouses linked to each other: the sample is restricted to self-employed whose spouses' primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment, and transfers to assisting spouses are partly recovered for 2002-2009 from spouses who are not self-employed.
Individuals linked over time into a panel 1994-2009, so that within-individual means of earned income and of retained earnings can be computed.
Income Tax Register linked to IDA for socioeconomic variables and the occupation classification.

sample.universe: The entire Danish population in the period 1994-2009 (high quality panel data compiled by Statistics Denmark, mainly from the Income Tax Register).
selection_rules: Only persons aged 25-59 years are considered.
Unless explicitly stated otherwise, only persons whose main occupation is self-employment are considered (workers are used as a comparison group in Figs. 1, 2 and 8).

For the entire sample 1994-2009, attention is restricted to self-employed whose spouses' primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment (because transfers to assisting spouses are only observed for 1994-2001, and only partly for 2002-2009).
The firm tax scheme and the capital returns scheme are treated as identical schemes.
For each Table 3 estimation sample, only self-employed observed at least three times are included.
sample.period: 1994-2009 (Table 3 estimation samples span 1996-2008; Fig. 3 extends back to 1987 using Tax Ministry figures)

construction_notes: The authors neither observe the distance to the tax cutoffs nor the marginal tax rates directly, and construct their own tax simulator taking special deductions and joint taxation of couples into account; for 95% of all individuals the simulated tax payments are within +/-5 DKK of the actual tax payments (p. 2).
Personal income is defined as the sum of wage earnings, declared firm profits (net of retained earnings), remunerations, provisions, alimony, etc. minus deductions (Fig. 1 note, p. 3).
Earned income is z_t = e_t + eta_t, i.e. effort-related income plus an additive component unaffected by effort (p. 6).
Adjusted earned income is z_t^adj = z_t - (eta_t - etabar); the income shock is estimated as eta_it - etabar_i = z_it - (1/T_i) sum_t z_it + (1/T_i) sum_t m_it (p. 10).
Incomes are divided into 1000 DKK bins and, in most figures, centred on the individual's effective tax bracket cutoff.
Excess masses are computed as in Saez (2010) with a bandwidth of delta = 7500 DKK: the share of individuals in a band of 7500 DKK around the kink minus the share in two surrounding bands.

Tax cutoffs differ between the six periods of Table 3 and are computed as the simple average within each period; marginal tax rates are the sample average marginal tax rates from the tax simulator, computed separately for the middle and the top bracket in each period.
Standard errors in Table 3 are block-bootstrapped at the individual level using 500 bootstrap samples.
Transfers to assisting spouses are observed directly for 1994-2001 and imputed for the second period, 2002-2008 (footnote 14, p. 15).
Self-employed are categorized into primary or secondary occupation self-employed using the variables pstill2 and sstill2, constructed by Statistics Denmark (Table 1 note, p. 6).

claims.statement: Excess mass (bunching) in taxable income at the top tax bracket cutoff, estimated on the 1996–2001 sample of Danish self-employed.

treatment.label: The kink in the piecewise linear personal income tax schedule at the top tax bracket cutoff (discrete jump in the marginal tax rate from τ_0 to τ_1 > τ_0)

register_source.value: Income Tax Register (Statistics Denmark), marginal tax rates and bracket cutoffs reconstructed with the authors' own tax simulator

definition.value: Personal income is taxed under a piecewise linear schedule with four brackets from 1996 onwards; at the top tax bracket cutoff the marginal tax rate jumps discretely (in 2001 from 49% to 63%). The authors neither observe the distance to the cutoffs nor the marginal tax rates directly and construct their own tax simulator, which replicates actual tax payments within +/−5 DKK for 95% of individuals.

timing.value: Contemporaneous: the kink faced in the income year in which income is measured; cutoffs are computed as the simple average over each estimation sub-period.

outcome.label: Excess mass (bunching) in taxable income at the top tax bracket cutoff

definition.value: Saez (2010) excess mass: the share of person-year observations with taxable income within ±7500 DKK of the top tax bracket cutoff minus the shares in the two adjacent bands [y*−2δ, y*−δ) and [y*+δ, y*+2δ), with δ = 7500 DKK (Eq. (5)). Taxable income is personal income: wage earnings, declared firm profits net of retained earnings, remunerations, provisions, alimony etc. minus deductions.

timing.value: Measured in each income year of the 1996–2001 estimation sample, relative to that period's average top tax bracket cutoff.

units.value: share of the estimation sample (fraction of person-year observations; 0.0683 = 6.83%)

magnitude.interpretation: a massive amount of bunching in taxable income with excess masses ranging from 6.83 to 9.22%

estimand.target_population: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 with self-employment as main occupation, observed at least three times in 1996–2001

population.description: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 whose main occupation is self-employment and whose spouse's primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment, observed in the population register panel 1994–2009.
population.selection: Persons aged 25–59; main occupation self-employment; spouse's primary or secondary occupation not self-employment; for the Table 3 estimation samples, self-employed observed at least three times.

identification.source_of_variation: The discrete jump in the marginal tax rate at the top tax bracket cutoff of the Danish piecewise linear personal income tax schedule, which creates a kink in the budget set; bunching of the income distribution at that kink identifies the behavioural response.

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass / trapezoid approximation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (5) and the note to Table 3: all excess masses are calculated as in Saez (2010); Figs. 2, 13 and 14 display the surrounding bands.

key_assumptions.assumption: The disutility of effort is iso-elastic and the structural elasticity ε is constant in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the paper notes the estimated excess mass would only be unaffected by income growth 'unless the structural elasticity is heterogeneous in the population' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: The marginal cost of intertemporal income shifting is zero, g′(m) = α = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.3: almost no bunching among self-employed who neither retain nor withdraw earnings (Fig. 8); a very small excess mass in earned income (Fig. 13); small potential gains from the personal income tax scheme.

key_assumptions.assumption: The ability parameter γ is individual specific and time constant.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues it is 'only a good approximation for shorter samples' and therefore cuts the sample period into halves and quarters.

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed withdraw all previously retained earnings by the end of the firm's lifetime, so retained earnings sum to zero over the planning horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as reasonable; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: No income uncertainty, no liquidity constraints and no discounting: the income components η_t are perfectly foreseen.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper later discusses liquidity constraints as a departure that downward-biases both estimators.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income components have mean zero among those above the kink in high income periods: E(η_t | γ ≥ γ_1^high) = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on age 25–59, on self-employment being the main occupation, on the spouse's primary or secondary occupation not being self-employment, and (in Table 3) on the individual being observed at least three times.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction in Section 2.1 and in the note to Table 3.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

estimator.value: Saez (2010) bunching estimator — excess mass around the top tax bracket kink, bandwidth δ = 7500 DKK; standard errors block-bootstrapped at the individual level using 500 bootstrap samples; implemented via Eq. (5)

estimation.specification: Excess mass at the top tax bracket cutoff, incomes binned in 1000 DKK bins and centred on the period-average cutoff; marginal tax rates are sample averages from the authors' tax simulator; Eq. (5)
estimation.clustering: Block bootstrap at the individual level, 500 bootstrap samples

source_table.value: Table 3, column 1996–2001, row 'Excess mass — Taxable income'

mediators_claimed: Retained earnings in the firm — the paper's claimed key margin facilitating bunching in taxable income

heterogeneity.finding: The excess masses and the elasticity estimates using taxable income are larger for the second half of the sample period (p. 15).
Bunching is massive and sharp for the self-employed and only a very small excess mass is found for wage earners (Figs. 1 and 2).

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: We therefore propose an extension to Saez' bunching formula that allows us to distinguish bunching based on real responses and pure income shifting.

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper later discusses liquidity constraints as a departure that downward-biases both estimators.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass / trapezoid approximation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (5) and the note to Table 3: all excess masses are calculated as in Saez (2010); Figs. 2, 13 and 14 display the surrounding bands.

key_assumptions.assumption: The disutility of effort is iso-elastic and the structural elasticity ε is constant in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the paper notes the estimated excess mass would only be unaffected by income growth 'unless the structural elasticity is heterogeneous in the population' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: The marginal cost of intertemporal income shifting is zero, g′(m) = α = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.3: almost no bunching among self-employed who neither retain nor withdraw earnings (Fig. 8); a very small excess mass in earned income (Fig. 13); small potential gains from the personal income tax scheme.

key_assumptions.assumption: The ability parameter γ is individual specific and time constant.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues it is 'only a good approximation for shorter samples' and therefore cuts the sample period into halves and quarters.

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed withdraw all previously retained earnings by the end of the firm's lifetime, so retained earnings sum to zero over the planning horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as reasonable; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: No income uncertainty, no liquidity constraints and no discounting: the income components η_t are perfectly foreseen.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper later discusses liquidity constraints as a departure that downward-biases both estimators.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income components have mean zero among those above the kink in high income periods: E(η_t | γ ≥ γ_1^high) = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on age 25–59, on self-employment being the main occupation, on the spouse's primary or secondary occupation not being self-employment, and (in Table 3) on the individual being observed at least three times.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction in Section 2.1 and in the note to Table 3.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

estimation.clustering: Block bootstrap at the individual level, 500 bootstrap samples

claims.statement: Structural elasticity ε estimated from the shifting areas around the cutoff (shifting method, Eq. (6)), estimated on the 1999–2001 sample of Danish self-employed.

treatment.label: The kink in the piecewise linear personal income tax schedule at the top tax bracket cutoff (discrete jump in the marginal tax rate from τ_0 to τ_1 > τ_0)

register_source.value: Income Tax Register (Statistics Denmark), marginal tax rates and bracket cutoffs reconstructed with the authors' own tax simulator

definition.value: Personal income is taxed under a piecewise linear schedule with four brackets from 1996 onwards; at the top tax bracket cutoff the marginal tax rate jumps discretely (in 2001 from 49% to 63%). The authors neither observe the distance to the cutoffs nor the marginal tax rates directly and construct their own tax simulator, which replicates actual tax payments within +/−5 DKK for 95% of individuals.

timing.value: Contemporaneous: the kink faced in the income year in which income is measured; cutoffs are computed as the simple average over each estimation sub-period.

outcome.label: Structural elasticity ε estimated from the shifting areas around the cutoff (shifting method, Eq. (6))

definition.value: The structural elasticity ε identified by subtracting the estimated mass of pure income shifters on both sides of the cutoff from the bunching mass in taxable income (Eq. (6)), bandwidth δ = 7500 DKK.

timing.value: Measured in each income year of the 1999–2001 estimation sample, relative to that period's average top tax bracket cutoff.

units.value: elasticity (unitless)

magnitude.interpretation: This leads us to conclude that the structural elasticity lies in the range of 0.14–0.20

estimand.target_population: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 with self-employment as main occupation, observed at least three times in 1999–2001

population.description: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 whose main occupation is self-employment and whose spouse's primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment, observed in the population register panel 1994–2009.
population.selection: Persons aged 25–59; main occupation self-employment; spouse's primary or secondary occupation not self-employment; for the Table 3 estimation samples, self-employed observed at least three times.

identification.source_of_variation: The discrete jump in the marginal tax rate at the top tax bracket cutoff of the Danish piecewise linear personal income tax schedule, which creates a kink in the budget set; bunching of the income distribution at that kink identifies the behavioural response.

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass / trapezoid approximation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (5) and the note to Table 3: all excess masses are calculated as in Saez (2010); Figs. 2, 13 and 14 display the surrounding bands.

key_assumptions.assumption: The disutility of effort is iso-elastic and the structural elasticity ε is constant in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the paper notes the estimated excess mass would only be unaffected by income growth 'unless the structural elasticity is heterogeneous in the population' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: The marginal cost of intertemporal income shifting is zero, g′(m) = α = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.3: almost no bunching among self-employed who neither retain nor withdraw earnings (Fig. 8); a very small excess mass in earned income (Fig. 13); small potential gains from the personal income tax scheme.

key_assumptions.assumption: The ability parameter γ is individual specific and time constant.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues it is 'only a good approximation for shorter samples' and therefore cuts the sample period into halves and quarters.

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed withdraw all previously retained earnings by the end of the firm's lifetime, so retained earnings sum to zero over the planning horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as reasonable; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: No income uncertainty, no liquidity constraints and no discounting: the income components η_t are perfectly foreseen.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper later discusses liquidity constraints as a departure that downward-biases both estimators.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income components have mean zero among those above the kink in high income periods: E(η_t | γ ≥ γ_1^high) = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on age 25–59, on self-employment being the main occupation, on the spouse's primary or secondary occupation not being self-employment, and (in Table 3) on the individual being observed at least three times.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction in Section 2.1 and in the note to Table 3.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

estimator.value: Saez (2010) bunching estimator — excess mass around the top tax bracket kink, bandwidth δ = 7500 DKK; standard errors block-bootstrapped at the individual level using 500 bootstrap samples; implemented via Eq. (6)

estimation.specification: Excess mass at the top tax bracket cutoff, incomes binned in 1000 DKK bins and centred on the period-average cutoff; marginal tax rates are sample averages from the authors' tax simulator; Eq. (6)
estimation.clustering: Block bootstrap at the individual level, 500 bootstrap samples

source_table.value: Table 3, column 1999–2001, row 'Adjusted earned income elasticity — Shifting method'

heterogeneity.finding: The excess masses and the elasticity estimates using taxable income are larger for the second half of the sample period (p. 15).
Bunching is massive and sharp for the self-employed and only a very small excess mass is found for wage earners (Figs. 1 and 2).

prior_findings_compared.citation: Saez, E., 2010. Do taxpayers bunch at kink points? Am. Econ. J. Econ. Policy 2, 180–212.
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: We therefore propose an extension to Saez' bunching formula that allows us to distinguish bunching based on real responses and pure income shifting.

Transfers to assisting spouses are only observed for 1994–2001 and are imputed for 2002–2009 (p. 2, footnote 14 p. 15)

regressors: ε (structural elasticity)
target_designation.reasoning: Table 3 is titled 'Elasticity estimates.' and its note states which equation each row estimates; the excess-mass rows are the inputs to those formulas.

anchor_quote.text: This leads us to conclude that the structural elasticity lies in the range of 0.14–0.20 and that the share of the bunching due to pure income shifting is in the interval between 52 and 68%

claims.statement: Share of the bunching mass in taxable income that is due to pure income shifting (bunching method, Eq. (4)), estimated on the 1996–2001 sample of Danish self-employed.

treatment.label: The kink in the piecewise linear personal income tax schedule at the top tax bracket cutoff (discrete jump in the marginal tax rate from τ_0 to τ_1 > τ_0)

register_source.value: Income Tax Register (Statistics Denmark), marginal tax rates and bracket cutoffs reconstructed with the authors' own tax simulator

definition.value: Personal income is taxed under a piecewise linear schedule with four brackets from 1996 onwards; at the top tax bracket cutoff the marginal tax rate jumps discretely (in 2001 from 49% to 63%). The authors neither observe the distance to the cutoffs nor the marginal tax rates directly and construct their own tax simulator, which replicates actual tax payments within +/−5 DKK for 95% of individuals.

timing.value: Contemporaneous: the kink faced in the income year in which income is measured; cutoffs are computed as the simple average over each estimation sub-period.

outcome.label: Share of the bunching mass in taxable income that is due to pure income shifting (bunching method, Eq. (4))

definition.value: The fraction of the observed excess mass in taxable income at the top tax bracket cutoff attributed to pure intertemporal income shifting rather than a real response, implied by the bunching method of Eq. (4).

timing.value: Measured in each income year of the 1996–2001 estimation sample, relative to that period's average top tax bracket cutoff.

units.value: share of the observed bunching mass in taxable income (fraction; 0.8285 = 82.85%)

magnitude.interpretation: the share of the bunching due to pure income shifting is in the interval between 52 and 68%

estimand.target_population: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 with self-employment as main occupation, observed at least three times in 1996–2001

population.description: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 whose main occupation is self-employment and whose spouse's primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment, observed in the population register panel 1994–2009.
population.selection: Persons aged 25–59; main occupation self-employment; spouse's primary or secondary occupation not self-employment; for the Table 3 estimation samples, self-employed observed at least three times.

identification.source_of_variation: The discrete jump in the marginal tax rate at the top tax bracket cutoff of the Danish piecewise linear personal income tax schedule, which creates a kink in the budget set; bunching of the income distribution at that kink identifies the behavioural response.

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass / trapezoid approximation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (5) and the note to Table 3: all excess masses are calculated as in Saez (2010); Figs. 2, 13 and 14 display the surrounding bands.

key_assumptions.assumption: The disutility of effort is iso-elastic and the structural elasticity ε is constant in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the paper notes the estimated excess mass would only be unaffected by income growth 'unless the structural elasticity is heterogeneous in the population' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: The marginal cost of intertemporal income shifting is zero, g′(m) = α = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.3: almost no bunching among self-employed who neither retain nor withdraw earnings (Fig. 8); a very small excess mass in earned income (Fig. 13); small potential gains from the personal income tax scheme.

key_assumptions.assumption: The ability parameter γ is individual specific and time constant.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues it is 'only a good approximation for shorter samples' and therefore cuts the sample period into halves and quarters.

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed withdraw all previously retained earnings by the end of the firm's lifetime, so retained earnings sum to zero over the planning horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as reasonable; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: No income uncertainty, no liquidity constraints and no discounting: the income components η_t are perfectly foreseen.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper later discusses liquidity constraints as a departure that downward-biases both estimators.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income components have mean zero among those above the kink in high income periods: E(η_t | γ ≥ γ_1^high) = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on age 25–59, on self-employment being the main occupation, on the spouse's primary or secondary occupation not being self-employment, and (in Table 3) on the individual being observed at least three times.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction in Section 2.1 and in the note to Table 3.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

estimator.value: Saez (2010) bunching estimator — excess mass around the top tax bracket kink, bandwidth δ = 7500 DKK; standard errors block-bootstrapped at the individual level using 500 bootstrap samples; implemented via Eq. (4)

estimation.specification: Excess mass at the top tax bracket cutoff, incomes binned in 1000 DKK bins and centred on the period-average cutoff; marginal tax rates are sample averages from the authors' tax simulator; Eq. (4)
estimation.clustering: Block bootstrap at the individual level, 500 bootstrap samples

source_table.value: Table 3, column 1996–2001, row 'Shifting share — Bunching method'

mediators_claimed: Retained earnings in the firm — the paper's claimed key margin facilitating bunching in taxable income

heterogeneity.finding: The excess masses and the elasticity estimates using taxable income are larger for the second half of the sample period (p. 15).
Bunching is massive and sharp for the self-employed and only a very small excess mass is found for wage earners (Figs. 1 and 2).

ambiguities: The paper summarises the shifting share as '50–70%' (p. 16) and 'between 52 and 68%' (p. 15); the individual Table 3 cells range from 0.4159 to 0.8285, so the summary range refers to the authors' preferred sub-periods, not to every cell.

evidence.how: The printed point estimate divided by the printed standard error exceeds 2 in absolute value; the paper itself prints no t-statistic, p-value or confidence interval for this cell.

identification.source_of_variation: The discrete jump in the marginal tax rate at the top tax bracket cutoff of the Danish piecewise linear personal income tax schedule, which creates a kink in the budget set; bunching of the income distribution at that kink identifies the behavioural response.

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass / trapezoid approximation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (5) and the note to Table 3: all excess masses are calculated as in Saez (2010); Figs. 2, 13 and 14 display the surrounding bands.

key_assumptions.assumption: The disutility of effort is iso-elastic and the structural elasticity ε is constant in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the paper notes the estimated excess mass would only be unaffected by income growth 'unless the structural elasticity is heterogeneous in the population' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: The marginal cost of intertemporal income shifting is zero, g′(m) = α = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.3: almost no bunching among self-employed who neither retain nor withdraw earnings (Fig. 8); a very small excess mass in earned income (Fig. 13); small potential gains from the personal income tax scheme.

key_assumptions.assumption: The ability parameter γ is individual specific and time constant.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues it is 'only a good approximation for shorter samples' and therefore cuts the sample period into halves and quarters.

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed withdraw all previously retained earnings by the end of the firm's lifetime, so retained earnings sum to zero over the planning horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as reasonable; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: No income uncertainty, no liquidity constraints and no discounting: the income components η_t are perfectly foreseen.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper later discusses liquidity constraints as a departure that downward-biases both estimators.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income components have mean zero among those above the kink in high income periods: E(η_t | γ ≥ γ_1^high) = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction in Section 2.1 and in the note to Table 3.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

identification.source_of_variation: The discrete jump in the marginal tax rate at the top tax bracket cutoff of the Danish piecewise linear personal income tax schedule, which creates a kink in the budget set; bunching of the income distribution at that kink identifies the behavioural response.

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass / trapezoid approximation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (5) and the note to Table 3: all excess masses are calculated as in Saez (2010); Figs. 2, 13 and 14 display the surrounding bands.

key_assumptions.assumption: The disutility of effort is iso-elastic and the structural elasticity ε is constant in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the paper notes the estimated excess mass would only be unaffected by income growth 'unless the structural elasticity is heterogeneous in the population' (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: The marginal cost of intertemporal income shifting is zero, g′(m) = α = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.3: almost no bunching among self-employed who neither retain nor withdraw earnings (Fig. 8); a very small excess mass in earned income (Fig. 13); small potential gains from the personal income tax scheme.

key_assumptions.assumption: The ability parameter γ is individual specific and time constant.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues it is 'only a good approximation for shorter samples' and therefore cuts the sample period into halves and quarters.

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-employed withdraw all previously retained earnings by the end of the firm's lifetime, so retained earnings sum to zero over the planning horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as reasonable; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: No income uncertainty, no liquidity constraints and no discounting: the income components η_t are perfectly foreseen.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper later discusses liquidity constraints as a departure that downward-biases both estimators.

key_assumptions.assumption: Income components have mean zero among those above the kink in high income periods: E(η_t | γ ≥ γ_1^high) = 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on age 25–59, on self-employment being the main occupation, on the spouse's primary or secondary occupation not being self-employment, and (in Table 3) on the individual being observed at least three times.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction in Section 2.1 and in the note to Table 3.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Bunching is not achieved primarily through (unobserved) tax evasion; if tax evasion were the only margin used to bunch, both estimators would be upward biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: More than 95% of the self-employed located at the top kink either retain or withdraw earnings; the very limited bunching in earned income; discussion of Kleven et al. (2011).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

population.description: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 whose main occupation is self-employment and whose spouse's primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment, observed in the population register panel 1994–2009.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass approximation).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).

treatment.label: The kink in the piecewise linear personal income tax schedule at the top tax bracket cutoff (discrete jump in the marginal tax rate from τ_0 to τ_1 > τ_0)

definition.value: Personal income is taxed under a piecewise linear schedule with four brackets from 1996 onwards; at the top tax bracket cutoff the marginal tax rate jumps discretely (in 2001 from 49% to 63%). estimand.target_population: Danish self-employed with self-employment as main occupation

population.description: Danish self-employed aged 25–59 whose main occupation is self-employment and whose spouse's primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment, observed in the population register panel 1994–2009.
population.selection: Persons aged 25–59; main occupation self-employment; spouse's primary or secondary occupation not self-employment; for the Table 3 estimation samples, self-employed observed at least three times.

identification.source_of_variation: The discrete jump in the marginal tax rate at the top tax bracket cutoff of the Danish piecewise linear personal income tax schedule.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on age 25–59, on self-employment being the main occupation, and on the spouse's primary or secondary occupation not being self-employment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as sample construction in Section 2.1.

implies_edges.to: taxable income relative to the top tax bracket cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual density of income around the kink is smooth and is approximated by the density in the two adjacent bands (the Saez (2010) excess-mass approximation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The note to Fig. 2 and to Table 3 state that excess masses are measured as in Saez (2010).

threats_discussed: Unobserved tax evasion: if bunching were achieved only by underdeclaring income both estimators would be upward biased (p. 11, p. 16).
Liquidity constraints: earnings can only be withdrawn if they were previously retained, which downward-biases both estimators and especially the bunching method of Eq. (4) (p. 11).
Unobserved adjustments of inventories and capital stock, which work like tax evasion (p. 11).
Endogenous conditioning on retained-earnings status when splitting the sample into retainers / withdrawers / neither (p. 12).
Longer estimation samples make the time-constant-ability assumption and perfect foresight less plausible and bias the adjusted-earned-income bunching estimator downwards (p. 10, p. 15).

Income growth relative to the tax bracket cutoff, the financial crisis, and learning about the post-1994 bracket structure as alternative explanations for the larger excess masses in the second half of the sample (p. 15).
robustness_checks: Bandwidth sensitivity: δ = 5000 DKK gives elasticities of 0.11–0.18 and δ = 10,000 DKK gives 0.15–0.20 (footnote 15, p. 15).
The sample period is cut into two halves and into four sub-periods (Table 3).
Self-employment is defined narrowly (primary occupation only), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation (p. 15).
Numerical simulations of the model confirm the two estimators agree in theory (footnote 10, p. 10).
Robustness of the estimators to modelled tax evasion that reduces earned income and retained earnings in parallel (p. 11).
unresolved_confounders: Tax evasion is unobserved in the data (p. 11).
Changes in inventories and capital stock are not observed (p. 11).
Small costs of transferring income (together with heterogeneous income shocks) cannot be distinguished from a low structural elasticity (p. 13).
The divergence between the bunching-method and shifting-method elasticity estimates is not resolved; the authors argue the truth is 'probably closer to 0.20 than to 0.14' (p. 15).
